a: An attempt to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a system or its data
A software update that goes wrong
A power cut in a server room
A network running slowly at busy times
tasks.fb: Damage, disruption and unauthorised access are the three things attackers are after.

a: Both outside the network and inside it
tasks.fb: Insiders, including careless staff, cause a large share of security incidents.

tasks.q: Match each form of attack to what it does.
pairs: Malicious software that damages or takes control of a system
Fake messages that trick people into giving away information
Trying huge numbers of passwords until one works
Flooding a server with requests so it can't respond
Capturing data as it travels across a network
Entering code into a text box to attack a database
tasks.fb: These six are the forms of attack named in the specification.

tasks.q: Why do most criminal cyberattacks happen?
tasks.fb: Ransom payments, fraud and selling stolen data all make money for attackers.

tasks.q: A pen tester is paid by a company to attack its systems. Is this a crime?
a: No, because the company has given permission
No, because no data is stored
tasks.fb: Permission is what separates penetration testing from criminal hacking.

tasks.q: What type of malware was CryptoLocker?
tasks.fb: It encrypted files and demanded payment for the key.

tasks.q: How did most victims get infected?
a: By opening an infected email attachment
tasks.fb: Email attachments are still one of the most common ways malware spreads.

a: An international operation that took down the botnet behind CryptoLocker
tasks.fb: It involved police forces, universities and security companies in several countries.

a: Attackers can operate from another country, hiding their identity and location
Attacks leave no trace at all
Police aren't allowed to investigate computers
tasks.fb: That's why investigations are international and take years.

tasks.q: Which of these are costs of a successful attack on a business? Select all that apply.
opts: Possible fines for failing to protect personal data
The price of new office furniture
correct: Possible fines for failing to protect personal data
tasks.fb: The ransom is often the smallest part of the total cost.

tasks.q: Which form of attack does each incident describe?
items: An email pretending to be from the bank asks for a password
Software downloaded with a game secretly deletes files
A program tries a million passwords on one account
A website is flooded with fake requests until it goes offline
A text message claims a parcel is waiting and links to a fake login page
A program encrypts files and demands a payment
Thousands of infected computers send traffic to one server at once
A dictionary of common passwords is tried against a login page
tasks.fb: Data interception and SQL injection come up in lessons 3 and 8.

info.title: White hats and black hats
info.text: Attackers who break in illegally are called black hats. White hats do the same thing with permission, to help organisations find weaknesses before criminals do.

info.title: Attacks per day
info.text: Large organisations see thousands of attempted attacks every day. Most are automated programs scanning for weaknesses, not people.

info.title: Hacktivism
info.text: Some attacks are political: groups attack organisations they disagree with to make a point. This is called hacktivism.

info.title: Paying doesn't help
info.text: Police advise against paying ransoms: it funds more crime and the files often stay locked. Good backups are a far better defence.

info.title: Still wanted
info.text: Evgeniy Bogachev is still on the FBI's most wanted cyber list, with a reward of up to $3 million.

info.title: The law
info.text: In the UK, the Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access to a computer system a crime, even if nothing is damaged.
